description: Flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes — the design tools used to plan IT products.
hero_image_caption: A designer sketching a wireframe layout on paper before building a digital product.
content_html:
Why Plan Before You Build?

Every successful IT product starts with a plan. Jumping straight into building a website, app or database without a design document wastes time and leads to costly mistakes. Design tools help developers, designers and clients agree on what the finished product should look like and how it should work — before a single line of code is written.

The exam requires you to know four main types of design tool: flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. For each one you must be able to describe its components, name software that creates it, and weigh up its advantages and disadvantages.

Key Fact

The four design tools are flow charts, mind maps, visualisation diagrams and wireframes. Each suits a different planning purpose — process logic, brainstorming, appearance, and page layout respectively.

Flow Charts

A flow chart maps out a process step by step. It uses internationally recognised symbols: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process steps), diamonds (decisions with yes/no branches) and parallelograms (input/output). Arrows show the direction of flow.

Flow charts are ideal when you need to show logic — for example, how a login system checks a username and password before granting access. Software such as Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart and even PowerPoint can create them, or they can be hand-sketched.

Advantages: clear visual representation of logic; easy for technical and non-technical stakeholders to follow; standard symbols mean the chart is understood internationally; helps identify missing steps or infinite loops before coding begins.

Disadvantages: can become very large and complex for multi-step systems; symbols must be used correctly or the diagram is misleading; updating a hand-drawn chart is time-consuming when the design changes.

Mind Maps

A mind map is a brainstorming tool. A central idea sits in the middle, with branches radiating outwards to related topics, and sub-branches adding more detail. The spec identifies three specific types used in IT design projects.

A library mind map organises a collection of resources or assets — for example, mapping all the images, audio clips and text files needed for a website. A tunnel timeline mind map sequences tasks over time, showing what must happen before the next stage can begin. A presentation mind map structures the content and flow of a presentation or report.

Mind maps can be drawn by hand or created using software such as MindMeister, Coggle or Microsoft Word’s SmartArt feature. They are quick to produce and easy to update as ideas evolve.

A visualisation diagram (sometimes called a mock-up) shows the intended appearance of an IT product. It includes colours, images, fonts and the general layout — it looks like the real thing but is not interactive. It is useful for getting client sign-off on aesthetics before development starts.

A wireframe is a skeletal layout of a single screen or web page. It uses simple boxes, placeholder text and labels to show where navigation menus, images, headings, forms and buttons will sit — but it deliberately avoids colour or imagery so the focus stays on structure and usability. Wireframes are often the first design step because they are quick to produce and cheap to revise.

Both can be created by hand or using specialist software. Tools widely used in schools and the workplace include Balsamiq (wireframes), Figma (visualisation diagrams) and PowerPoint or Google Slides (both).

Key Fact

A flow chart uses four standard shapes: ovals (start/end), rectangles (process), diamonds (decision) and parallelograms (input/output). Using these symbols correctly is essential — the examiner rewards labelled, accurate designs.

Sketches vs Software

Design tools can be created either by hand (sketching on paper) or using software. Each approach has its place. Hand sketches are fast, require no technology, and are ideal for early-stage brainstorming when ideas are still forming. They are also exactly what the exam’s 8-mark “create” question requires — students hand-draw their design solution.

Software-created designs look more professional, are easier to share with clients and team members, and are much simpler to edit when changes are needed. The trade-off is that software takes longer to learn and requires access to the correct application. In a professional project, hand sketches are typically used first and then refined digitally.

Assessing Suitability

Choosing the right design tool for a given context is a key exam skill. Ask yourself: does the project need to show a process or logic (flow chart), explore ideas or assets (mind map), communicate intended appearance (visualisation diagram) or plan page structure (wireframe)? A scenario question might describe a developer building a new booking system — a flow chart suits the booking logic, a wireframe suits the booking form layout, and a visualisation diagram suits the client sign-off on colours and branding.
exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark “create” question you will be asked to hand-sketch a design tool for a given scenario — often a mind map, flow chart or wireframe. The biggest mark losses come from missing labels and diagrams that ignore the scenario. Use all four standard flow chart symbols if you draw a flow chart, label every branch of a mind map, and annotate every section of a wireframe. Examiners reward completeness, correct use of symbols and a clear link back to the named scenario — not artistic quality.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four design tools are flow charts (showing logic/process), mind maps (brainstorming/organising — three types: library, tunnel timeline, presentation), visualisation diagrams (showing appearance) and wireframes (showing page structure).
  • Design tools can be created by hand or using software; hand sketches are faster and used in the exam, software versions are more professional and easier to share or update.
  • Matching the right tool to the right context is a key exam skill — process logic needs a flow chart, page layout needs a wireframe, client aesthetics need a visualisation diagram.

practice_questions.text: Which design tool uses a diamond shape to represent a decision point?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Flow chart (only). Distractor check: Mind map (no — uses branches), Wireframe (no — uses boxes/placeholders), Visualisation diagram (no — shows appearance without process symbols).

practice_questions.text: Identify one component found in a wireframe.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: any one of — placeholder boxes for images; navigation menu labels; content area boundaries; button placeholders; heading position markers. Accept any clearly named structural element. Do not accept colour or imagery (these are absent from wireframes by definition).

practice_questions.text: Outline what a visualisation diagram is used for.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: shows what the finished IT product will look like (1) including colours, fonts, images and layout (1). Award 1 mark for a partial description that identifies appearance without enough detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of using software to create a design tool rather than sketching it by hand.
practice_questions.marks: Advantage (1 mark): any one of — easier to edit when design changes; looks more professional; easier to share digitally with clients/team; can undo mistakes instantly. Disadvantage (1 mark): any one of — requires access to the correct software; takes longer to learn; may not be available in all settings. Award 1 mark per distinct, described point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a developer planning a user login system would choose a flow chart rather than a mind map.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): identifies flow chart is suited to showing logic/process (1), explains that the login system involves a decision (e.g. is the password correct?) with two outcomes (yes/no branches) (1), and explains why this matters (e.g. because mind maps do not show decision branches or process order, so the logic would be unclear) (1).
Secure (2): identifies the correct tool and gives a reason linked to logic or decisions but without full development.
Developing (1): names the tool only, or gives a generic advantage of flow charts without connecting to the login scenario.
Emerging (0): no creditworthy content.

practice_questions.text: On the page, sketch a mind map for a small IT company planning a new e-commerce website. Your mind map should include: the central topic; at least four main branches; at least two sub-branches on each main branch; and clear labels throughout.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): central topic clearly labelled (1); four or more distinct, relevant main branches (e.g. design, content, security, testing, payment, user accounts) (2); at least two labelled sub-branches per main branch (2); labels are specific to e-commerce context (1); diagram is clear and well-organised with no unlabelled nodes (1); overall completeness relative to brief (1).
Secure (5–6): most criteria met; minor omissions in sub-branches or labelling.
Developing (3–4): central topic present; fewer than four branches or sub-branches largely missing or unlabelled.
Emerging (1–2): partial attempt — central idea present but very limited branching or labels.
0: no creditworthy attempt.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of mind map is used to organise a collection of resources or assets for a project?
A flow chart diamond shape represents which of the following?
options: The start or end of a process

knowledge_checks.q: A _____ shows the structural layout of a screen using placeholder boxes and labels, without colour or detailed imagery.
Creating a design tool by hand is faster and requires no technology, but a _____ version is easier to share and edit.
Match each design tool to its main purpose.
right: Shows intended colours, fonts and appearance
Maps process logic using standard symbols
Brainstorms ideas radiating from a central topic
Plans page structure using placeholder boxes

flashcard_questions.q: What shape represents a decision in a flow chart?
What shape represents a process step in a flow chart?
What shape represents start or end in a flow chart?
Name the three types of mind map in the spec.
What does a library mind map organise?
flashcard_questions.a: A collection of resources or assets.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a wireframe deliberately leave out?
flashcard_questions.a: Colour and detailed imagery — focuses on structure only.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a visualisation diagram show that a wireframe does not?
flashcard_questions.a: The intended final appearance including colours and fonts.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of hand-sketching a design tool.
flashcard_questions.a: Fast to produce and requires no technology.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one advantage of software-created design tools.
flashcard_questions.a: Easier to edit after design changes.

flashcard_questions.q: Which design tool is best suited to planning the logic of a login system?
flashcard_questions.a: Flow chart — it shows decisions and process order.

flashcard_questions.q: Which design tool would a client use to approve colours and branding before development?

glossary_terms.definition: Documents created before building an IT solution to plan its structure, content and appearance.
A diagram that uses standard shapes and arrows to show the steps and decisions in a process.
A branching diagram that places a central idea in the middle and radiates related topics, subtopics and details outwards.
A design tool that shows what a finished IT product will look like, including colours, images, fonts and layout, but without working functionality.
A basic structural plan of a web page or screen that shows the position of elements such as navigation menus, content areas and buttons, without colour or detailed design.
